ai-bfa998e6f2.headline: India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity
ai-bfa998e6f2.fulltext:
AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday.
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.”
The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.”
This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal.
At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around.
Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers.
CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information.
For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords.
In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity.

ai-1a106cb757.headline: Meta releases Muse Spark Open, a new ‘open-weight’ AI model
ai-1a106cb757.fulltext:
Meta on Thursday launched a new open-weight AI model which it claims rivals, and in some cases outperforms, similar products from leading Chinese developers.
Muse Spark Open “is the most capable US open-weight model to date,” Meta’s chief of AI Alexandr Wang wrote on X.
Unlike so-called closed models – such as Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT – developers can download the parameters, known as weights and biases, of an open-weight model and modify them.
Chinese developers have emerged as dominant players in the open-weight market for AI models over the past couple of years.
Alibaba’s Qwen, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Z.ai’s GLM models have been considered open-weight frontrunners globally, but Meta claims its new open model now competes on a similar level.
“Built for coding and agentic work,” Muse Spark Open “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning,” Meta said in a blogpost, adding that “strong safeguards” have been integrated into the new model.
Muse Spark Open is also “optimized” to run on Apple’s advanced M5 Ultra chips, Meta said, signaling an unusual partnership between the two tech companies.
Muse Spark Open requires significant computing power. Users can run the model on two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra chips to create a “supercomputer” on their own desktop, Meta said.
The launch comes just days after Meta announced its newest closed model, which it said rivalled the most advanced versions of ChatGPT and Claude.
Meta’s AI efforts were initially focused on open models, but more recently Zuckerberg has pushed the company to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic.

india-deep-tech-b6d2e11303.headline: Nandan Nilekani-backed F2A raises ₹3,000 cr for AI, deeptech fund; hard cap raised to ₹3,500 cr
india-deep-tech-b6d2e11303.fulltext:
Fundamentum Frontier Advisors (F2A), which counts Nandan Nilekani as its anchor investor, has secured aggregate subscriptions of ₹3,000 crore for a growth-stage AI and deeptech fund and raised its hard cap to ₹3,500 crore on strong demand.
Indian and overseas investors have put in money in a 70:30 ratio through two regulated vehicles, F2A General Partner Ashish Kumar told PTI. Total demand for the fund is more than ₹3,500 crore, he said.
"We have already closed subscriptions of ₹3,000 crore and have a total demand in excess of ₹3,500 crore at this time. We are negotiating with a few select investors from the oversubscriptions while deciding the final allocations for the remaining ₹500 crore and will make a final close soon after," Kumar said.
The money from overseas comes mostly from institutions, while the Indian investors include institutions, corporates and family offices. Nilekani, the fund's anchor investor and mentor, has taken the maximum allocation reserved for family trusts, Kumar said, without specifying the amount.
Terming the fund as India's largest dedicated growth-stage AI and deep tech fund, F2A plans to deploy the corpus across 12-15 investments over the next two to three years, with cheques of ₹100-200 crore each.
Kumar said the larger fund size would not mean more companies. Instead, it would give the entity room for slightly larger cheques and bigger follow-on investments in its best-performing companies.
F2A is in advanced stages of closing three investments over the next quarter. All three are early-growth-stage companies, with initial cheques of ₹100-170 crore, Kumar said. Two are in deep tech infrastructure, and one is in enterprise AI.
"Out of the 12-15 companies, we anticipate deep tech infrastructure and digital consumer to account for 40 per cent of the allocation each, with enterprise software taking the remaining 20 per cent. Some of the companies will fall into multiple categories, and we expect at least 50 per cent of allocation overall to companies with deep technology IP," he said.
Within deeptech, the fund will focus on areas in the AI value chain, such as semiconductors, the AI compute supply chain, robotics, defence and advanced materials.
"Any company that doesn't intend to own any part of the supply chain will be avoided," Kumar said.
F2A will invest only in India-domiciled companies. It will also work with Indian founders who start companies abroad and, where relevant, encourage them to move back to India, he said.
"We believe India and the US will create companies with different architectures, and we are looking to back companies that have structural advantages to be in India - either because of captive demand, domain understanding or specific talent density," Kumar said.
In AI, the fund will also consider foundation-model companies, but only differentiated models that trade breadth of use for greater efficiency of resources, he added.
Apart from capital, F2A plans to help its portfolio companies with go-to-market support and engaging with policymakers, Kumar said.
In May 2026, Nandan Nilekani's VC firm Fundamentum Partnership launched F2A, a dedicated frontier-tech investment platform. Founded in 2017, Fundamentum is a growth-stage investment firm and has backed companies such as PharmEasy, Spinny, KukuFM, Wishlink and Olyv.

indian-startups-765f290a52.headline: Rising AI’s Costs Put SaaS Companies Between A Rock And A Hard Place
indian-startups-765f290a52.fulltext: Recently, Zoho cofounder Sridhar Vembu raised concerns over the economics of building software in an AI-driven market. In a post on X, Vembu said server prices have risen 4-5X in a year, while AI usage and token expenditure are pushing up operating costs. Zoho, however, plans to respond by cutting its marketing budget, freezing headcount for 18 months and pausing its usual salary hikes this year. Vembu’s concern is that while AI has made software easier to build, running a software business is getting more expensive. At the same time, AI coding tools and agents are challenging traditional subscription and per-seat pricing models. Another concern, as per Vembu, is that AI-driven productivity gains in software development currently stand at 25% to 50% when measured across the entire product development process. While developers can build prototypes faster, testing, verification and other stages of taking a product to market continue to require human involvement. When AI Costs Start To Bite As AI eats into SaaS revenue, it is also making software more expensive to run. Every AI query requires computing power, adding to operating costs. At the same time, growing demand for AI infrastructure is driving up hardware prices, making it more expensive for companies to run their software. According to ICONIQ’s 2026 data, AI products have an average gross margin of around 52%, compared with the 80% benchmark for traditional SaaS. For established SaaS companies adding AI features, gross margins can fall by 12-17 percentage points, depending on how efficiently they manage AI computing costs. The pressure is also forcing software companies to reconsider how much profitability they are willing to sacrifice to build AI products. On October 15, 2026, SaaS giant Figma’s CFO, Praveer Melwani, said the design software company might not return to its previous gross margins of over 90% as it invests in AI features. Its margins were in the mid-80% range, with the company prioritising long-term growth and competitiveness over an immediate return to earlier profitability levels, according to Reuters. Meanwhile, rather than treating every decline as a problem to be eliminated, some software companies are accepting higher costs, expecting AI features will attract more users, strengthen their products and create future revenue opportunities. Similarly, some are adding more capabilities without proportionately increasing subscription prices. Krish Ramineni, cofounder and CEO of Fireflies, said that the company has not raised its subscription pricing in the five to six years since launching its meeting note-taking product. It is now expanding beyond meeting notes into tasks such as summarising emails, responding to workplace messages and preparing users for meetings, while aiming to include more tools within a single subscription. The Push To Rein In AI Spending The pressure to manage AI expenditure is also showing up in the financial results of Indian companies. Groww, for example, reported a 28% year-on-year increase in total expenses to ₹556 Cr in Q2 FY27, even as revenue from operations grew 47% to ₹1,501 Cr. In its shareholder letter, the company identified inflation in compute costs due to AI adoption as one factor behind higher serving costs. Cofounder and CFO Ishan Bansal said AI-related costs began rising as the company increased its focus on AI, alongside higher compute usage on trading days and a one-off operational expense. Groww expects inflation-driven costs to remain part of its operational baseline going forward. This is prompting companies to re-evaluate their technology investments. Instead of relying entirely on large, general-purpose models, some are fine-tuning smaller models for specific tasks, optimising infrastructure and using more expensive models only when necessary. Perfios, a financial technology company serving banks and other financial institutions, is taking this approach to manage the cost of deploying AI. Sumit Nigam, chief technology officer at Perfios, said the company is fine-tuning smaller language models and optimising model and GPU architecture to make specific workloads cheaper to run. According to him, GPU utilisation costs for some use cases have become significantly lower than the cost of relying on external models such as Google’s Gemini or Anthropic’s Claude. Companies are also looking to improve visibility into how AI expenditure builds up across teams, applications and workflows. On October 12, US-based software company Freshworks signed an agreement to acquire Torii, a software management platform. The deal is intended to extend Freshworks’ Freshservice product into software management and AI spend governance. Torii tracks software applications, licences and AI consumption and attributes spending to the people and teams driving it. The platform is designed to help IT and finance teams understand what is being used, identify cost spikes, set limits and forecast expenditure. Perfios, meanwhile, is combining cost optimisation with closer scrutiny of business returns. Sridhar Narayan, chief business officer at Perfios, said the company tracks profitability at both the product and customer levels. The focus is on optimising costs and directing spending towards areas where it can deliver better business outcomes, rather than cutting expenditure indiscriminately. These approaches point to two parts of AI cost management: making usage visible and controllable, and reducing the cost of delivering each AI-powered task. While AI is making software cheaper to build, the real value lies in data, workflows, integrations and the ability to run business processes reliably at scale. Adapting To A New AI Reality As Indian technology companies head into 2027, they face a two-sided challenge: customers are demanding more productivity from AI, while companies must figure out how to earn sustainable revenues. For IT services firms, this is changing how clients pay for work. A Reuters report found that AI is pushing clients to link payments to productivity gains rather than the hours billed by IT services companies, forcing the industry to rethink its pricing models. For SaaS companies, the challenge is different. As AI makes software easier and cheaper to build, products with limited differentiation risk becoming easier to replace. According to Prashant Singh, the cofounder and COO of LeadSquared, “If AI makes software cheaper to build, then software that was only ever an interface over a database becomes harder to defend. That pressure is real.” But Singh believes the threat is not uniform across the industry. “What is being commoditised is the ability to build an application, not the ability to run a business process reliably at scale,” he said. Proprietary data, integrations and industry-specific workflows will continue to help companies retain their competitive edge. Going into 2027, the challenge for Indian tech companies will be to adapt to AI-driven changes in pricing and customer expectations while protecting their margins.

climate-energy-a104a6b722.headline: U.S. trade commission finds solar imports from India, Indonesia and Laos are harming domestic industry
climate-energy-a104a6b722.fulltext:
U.S. trade commission finds solar imports from India, Indonesia and Laos are harming domestic industry
The U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC) has issued a final affirmative injury determination in its Solar IV investigation targeting crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells, whether or not assembled into modules, imported from India, Indonesia, and Laos.
The decision clears the final legal hurdle for federal trade protection, finding that dumped and subsidized imports from the three Asian nations cause material injury to domestic solar manufacturers. As a direct result of the ruling, the U.S. Department of Commerce will issue official antidumping (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) orders, establishing high tariff barriers and permanent cash deposit requirements across all three import corridors.
The upcoming duty orders will impose combined tariff rates as high as 249% for India, 268% for Indonesia, and 219% for Laos. These case-specific remedies, governed by the Tariff Act of 1930, will stack directly on top of existing executive tariffs and Section 232 minimum import price floors rather than replacing them.
Finalized duty rates
The USITC vote locks in the final margins established by Commerce last month. For Indian suppliers, Commerce set final dumping margins at 123.04% for all producers alongside a countervailing subsidy rate of 126.09%. Indonesian exporters face final dumping margins set at 94.36% for all producers, with countervailing duty rates ranging between 73.2% and 173.7% depending on the specific supplier. For imports originating in Laos, Commerce established final dumping margins at 65.43% for all exporters, accompanied by countervailing subsidy rates ranging between 82.03% and 153.67%.
The trade cases were originally brought by the Alliance for American Solar Manufacturing and Trade, a coalition represented by lead petitioners First Solar, Hanwha Qcells USA, and Mission Solar Energy. The litigation follows earlier Solar III duty orders targeting Southeast Asian manufacturing hubs in Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam.
Next steps
Following the USITC’s final injury determination, Commerce is scheduled to issue its official AD and CVD orders in early November 2026. Upon publication, U.S. Customs and Border Protection will be instructed to require final duty cash deposits on all incoming entries of cells and modules from India, Indonesia, and Laos.
The Commission’s full public report, Crystalline Silicon Photovoltaic Cells, Whether or Not Assembled Into Modules, from India, Indonesia, and Laos (Inv. Nos. 701-TA-772-774 and 731-TA-1756-1758, USITC Publication 5804) detailing its factual findings and legal analysis, will be published on the USITC website by November 23, 2026.

india-3ca7c05df8.headline: [Inquiry & Insights] UPI's 0.4 Percent MDR: Who Pays for India's Digital Payments?
india-3ca7c05df8.fulltext:
For years, UPI has underpinned a digital payments system in which transactions are quick, convenient and, for merchants, effectively free. From 15 October 2026, that model changes. For specified UPI merchant payments above ₹2,000, merchants will pay a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) at 0.4 percent of the transaction value, capped at ₹300 per transaction.
The government has also barred merchants from passing the MDR on to customers. Enforcing this prohibition can prevent a separate UPI surcharge, but merchants could still recover some costs through general prices. Who pays the fee is therefore distinct from who ultimately bears its cost.
The more important question is who ultimately pays for India's digital payment infrastructure. India's new UPI pricing regime places that question at the centre of the debate.
How Low Is 0.4 Percent?
By comparison with many US credit-card fees, India's 0.4 percent MDR is relatively low. US credit-card interchange rates vary by card and merchant category, with many exceeding 1 percent before other merchant charges are included. The European Union caps interchange fees at 0.2 percent for consumer debit cards and 0.3 percent for consumer credit cards, but these caps do not cover the total cost of card acceptance.
Card fees provide context, but different services and cost structures limit the comparison. They do not, by themselves, establish whether India's 0.4 percent MDR is appropriate.
What Does 0.4 Percent Mean for Merchants?
The policy limits smaller merchants' exposure: those receiving up to ₹1 lakh a month through UPI QR payments under the P2PM category are exempt. The Finance Ministry estimates that 96 percent of merchant UPI transactions will remain unaffected because they are either within the ₹2,000 threshold or covered by the small-merchant exemption. This figure refers to transaction numbers, not transaction value.
Certain sectors have separate rates. Eligible payments above ₹2,000 in sectors including railways, telecommunications, insurance, fuel and agricultural inputs attract a flat ₹5 MDR; capital-market payments attract 0.02 percent, capped at ₹300.
DMart, one of India's largest grocery retailers, reported a net profit margin of 4.8 percent for the year ending March 2026. A 0.4 percent fee would therefore amount to about 8.3 percent of its net margin if applied across sales. For merchants with lower margins, the same rate could have a larger effect. The economic significance of the MDR will therefore depend on both the share of a merchant's sales subject to the fee and the margin available to absorb it.
Who Pays for a Payment System?
In January 2020, the government eliminated MDR on BHIM-UPI and RuPay debit-card transactions. It subsequently introduced incentives to support payment-system participants. Combined incentive payouts for UPI and RuPay rose from ₹1,389 crore in FY 2021–22 to ₹3,631 crore in FY 2023–24.
The Budget Estimate for the incentive scheme was ₹437 crore in FY 2025–26, subsequently increased to about ₹2,196 crore in the Revised Estimate. The Budget Estimate for FY 2026–27 is ₹2,000 crore.
In September 2026, National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) Managing Director and CEO Dilip Asbe estimated UPI's annual cost to the banking system at around ₹21,000 crore, substantially above the government's incentive payments.
These costs suggest that some expenditure has been absorbed within the payment ecosystem. The new MDR changes this financing model by assigning part of that cost directly to merchants.
Alternate Models of Public Payment Infrastructure
Brazil's Pix, launched in November 2020, offers a different institutional model from UPI. Pix is operated by Brazil's central bank, which also sets the rules governing the system. A 2022 Bank for International Settlements study reported an average merchant cost of 0.22 percent per transaction, below India's proposed 0.4 percent MDR.
Thailand's PromptPay is another central-bank-led instant payment system. The World Bank highlights its integration into everyday public payments, including bill payments, government welfare transfers and tax refunds. Its role therefore extends beyond the merchant-payment use that dominates the current debate over UPI.
A New Financing Model for UPI
The 0.4 percent MDR therefore matters for what it signals: a shift in who finances India's digital payment infrastructure. As UPI moves from a model involving public support and costs absorbed within the payment ecosystem towards greater merchant contribution, assessing the policy requires more than comparing headline rates.
The relevant tests are the costs being recovered, how fee revenue is allocated, merchants' actual exposure and the effect on continued acceptance. A financing model that supports reliable infrastructure while sustaining merchant participation would strengthen UPI.

india-deep-tech-5603fc3cb3.headline: DRDO Tests Quantum Shield for Weapon-Trial Data
india-deep-tech-5603fc3cb3.fulltext:
The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has configured and tested a Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) platform on the live network of its dynamic test ranges at the Proof & Experimental Establishment (PXE) in Chandipur, Odisha. The system is intended to protect critical observations and telemetry generated during artillery and armoured-weapon testing, DRDO said in a statement on October 14.
Telemetry is the stream of measurements sent back by instruments during a test. It can include readings such as a projectile’s speed, trajectory and impact point-information that can reveal how a weapon performs. Protecting those data flows matters because unauthorised access could expose sensitive technical findings.
QKD is designed to help secure the exchange of cryptographic keys-the secret values used to encrypt and decrypt information. In a fibre-based QKD link, quantum signals carry key information. Because measuring those signals can disturb them, the communicating parties can detect signs of interception and take steps such as rejecting a compromised key. QKD does not encrypt the underlying trial data by itself; it supplies keys for encryption systems that protect the data.
DRDO says the platform was developed under its Microelectronic Devices, Computational Systems & Cyber Security (MCC) cluster, with Bengaluru-based Taqbit Labs as production partner. The organisation described the system as offering eavesdropping detection and “unconditional security”. In practical terms, QKD’s security properties are based on quantum physics rather than on the assumption that an attacker lacks sufficient computing power.
The Chandipur deployment follows earlier work to take the technology beyond laboratory demonstrations. In February 2022, DRDO and Indian Institute of Technology-Delhi scientists demonstrated a QKD link of more than 100 kilometres between Prayagraj and Vindhyachal in Uttar Pradesh, according to the report. In June 2025, they demonstrated transmission of quantum keys through open air over more than one kilometre on the IIT-Delhi campus, an approach that could be useful where fibre links are difficult to install.
In July 2026, DRDO and Taqbit Labs completed military field trials of a scalable, fibre-based QKD system. The latest test marks a further step: applying the platform on the operational network of a defence test range, rather than only demonstrating a link under trial conditions. The report does not specify the Chandipur network’s link length, key-generation rate or whether the system is intended for broader deployment.
PXE’s Chandipur range extends along the Odisha coast and out to sea, where artillery, rockets and armoured systems are evaluated. A secure channel for test observations could help protect sensitive results as they move between measurement equipment and analysts, while interception alerts could prompt operators to discard compromised keys and establish a fresh exchange.
The work also fits within India’s broader effort to build quantum technologies. The National Quantum Mission, approved in 2023 with an outlay of ₹6,003.65 crore for 2023-24 to 2030-31, includes development of satellite-based secure quantum communications, according to the report. Its stated ambition is to support secure quantum links over distances of up to 2,000 kilometres.
The Chandipur test demonstrates a defence use for quantum-secured communications, but it is not evidence that quantum encryption is already protecting all military networks. Wider use would depend on engineering, network integration and reliable operation beyond a single test-range setting. For now, DRDO’s announcement points to a practical objective: safeguarding weapon-test data and making attempts to tap the key-exchange link detectable.

deep-tech-bc0a4839e7.headline: Gaganyaan: ISRO completes key test ahead of first uncrewed mission
deep-tech-bc0a4839e7.fulltext:
Separating the crew module from the service module involves multiple precisely sequenced separation events with pyrotechnic devices and jettisoning systems
Ahead of the first uncrewed mission of the Gaganyaan (G1) which is targeted for launch this year, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has completed a series of Crew Module (CM)-Service Module (SM) separation tests for the Gaganyaan missions.
The Gaganyaan Orbital Module comprises the CM and SM which are connected using a separation system.
Electrical and fluid servicing between CM and SM is ensured through umbilical connections. These modules are integrated prior to the launch and function as a single integrated module from launch till the completion of the on-orbit phase of the mission.
Prior to commencing re-entry into the earth’s atmosphere, the CM is separated from the SM.
Separation of the CM from the SM involves multiple precisely sequenced separation events involving pyrotechnic devices and jettisoning systems.
The ISRO said that in order to validate the overall design adequacy of the separation system, a test setup was realised at the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, Thiruvananthapuram, for simulating the overall CM-SM assembly with extensive instrumentation.
“The tests simulated the scenario of the CM-SM separation involving the severing of several umbilical connections between the CM and SM. Besides validating the design adequacy of the overall CM-SM separation systems, these tests have also demonstrated robustness and shock-survivability of various critical subsystems in the CM,” the space agency said.
These include various avionics systems, inertial navigation systems, thermal protection system in the Aft and conical heat shield, crew module deployable umbilical shield as well as pyrotechnic devices of crew module uprighting system and thermal and humidity control system.
The ISRO said that this test provides necessary confidence in the functioning of the implemented CM-SM separation system for the upcoming G1 mission.
The Gaganyaan mission envisages demonstration of human spaceflight capability by launching a crew of three members to an orbit of 400 km for a three-day mission and bringing them back safely to earth, by landing in Indian sea waters.

PUNE, October 16: Muks Robotics, a Pune-based humanoid robotics company, has secured a project with the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) to develop SPACEO Prime, India's first humanoid space worker. The project marks a milestone in the Indian Space Economy...
PUNE, October 16: Muks Robotics, a Pune-based humanoid robotics company, has secured a project with the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) to develop SPACEO Prime, India's first humanoid space worker. The project marks a milestone in the Indian Space Economy to develop intelligent robots capable of operating in space.
As space missions become increasingly complex, robotic systems could play an important role in assisting astronauts, performing demanding operations and handling tasks in hazardous environments. For Muks Robotics, the project represents progress towards a vision first conceived by its founder, Dr. Mukesh Bangar, in 2021: building humanoids not just for Earth, but also for space.
Muks Robotics is a Pune-based startup, working towards the development of humanoid robots and Physical AI systems designed to perceive their surroundings, understand instructions, and perform tasks in real-world environments.
Developing a humanoid for space-related applications presents challenges beyond conventional robotics. Mobility, manipulation, autonomy, and reliability must be considered alongside the demands of the intended operating environment. The ISRO project provides an opportunity for Muks Robotics to build indigenous humanoids in alignment with "Atmanirbhar Bharat," strengthening India's self-reliance in advanced robotics and contributing to the nation's vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.
At the centre of the company's journey is Dr. Mukesh Bangar, Founder and CEO of Muks Robotics. A self-taught AI and robotics engineer, Dr. Bangar is focused on developing intelligent robotic systems capable of understanding their surroundings, learning autonomously, and performing meaningful physical tasks.
"I firmly believe that true freedom from pain and suffering (Moksh) can be achieved through self-sustaining autonomous robots. Moreover, now is the right time to deploy conscious, intelligent robots to other planets to safeguard the future of our existence," says Dr. Mukesh Bangar.
In 2021, his vision began taking shape around a long-term ambition to build humanoids for Earth and beyond. The company subsequently presented its mission and vision through a video in 2023, outlining its direction in humanoid robotics and its ambition to extend robotic capabilities beyond Earth.
The development of the SPACEO platform created a foundation for pursuing this ambition. The ISRO project represents a significant step towards translating that vision into a dedicated humanoid development effort, bringing the company closer to its goal of developing robots capable of supporting human activities in space.
The development of SPACEO Prime aligns with India's Make in India initiative and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision of Viksit Bharat 2047, which aims to transform India into a developed nation by the centenary of its independence. The vision emphasises self-reliance, innovation and indigenous technological advancement.
With established capabilities in satellite technology, launch systems and planetary exploration, India is well-positioned to expand into advanced robotics, artificial intelligence and autonomous systems. For Muks Robotics, SPACEO Prime represents an effort to develop advanced humanoid technology in India and contribute to the country's growing deep-tech ecosystem. However, developing a space-oriented humanoid requires rigorous testing, reliability and safety to meet the demanding conditions of space missions.
Humanoid robots could offer advantages in environments designed around human tools, workstations, and equipment. Their articulated arms and human-like body structure could potentially enable them to manipulate objects, handle tools, and interact with existing infrastructure.
Future applications could include equipment inspection, maintenance assistance, material handling, and other repetitive or hazardous tasks. Such systems could help reduce astronauts' exposure to certain risks and support mission operations.
These possibilities depend on the robot's capabilities, engineering validation, and mission requirements. They represent the broader potential of humanoid space robotics rather than confirmed operational capabilities of SPACEO Prime.
Muks Robotics aims to build humanoids for practical applications on Earth while developing the technological foundations for future work beyond the planet.
SPACEO Prime brings together this long-term vision and an opportunity to contribute to India's space technology ambitions. Moving from development to actual space operations will require sustained engineering, testing, and validation.
For a robotics company based in Pune, the ambition now extends beyond conventional workplaces. With a vision of extending its mission to the Moon and Mars as well. What began as a vision in 2021 is taking shape as a dedicated development effort, with the potential to expand the role of Indian-built humanoid technology beyond Earth.
For Muks Robotics, the goal is not simply to build a machine that resembles a human, but to develop one that could help humans work in places where they have never worked before.

Chinese chip and tech firms have flagged as much as six-fold growth in unaudited third-quarter profits, as huge demand for home-grown processors and artificial intelligence infrastructure filters through links in the supply chain amid the country’s push for self-reliance.
Shanghai-listed Yuanjie Semiconductor Technology expected its quarterly net profit to land between 403 million yuan and 453 million yuan, up 579 per cent to 660 per cent from a year earlier.
The maker of laser chips for optical communications said data-centre demand was driving shipments and helping maintain high margins.
Some public firms offered a glimpse of their financial performance in the first nine months of the year, ahead of final third-quarter results announcements.
Graphics processing unit (GPU) designer MetaX, listed in Shanghai but also pursuing a Hong Kong listing, turned a profit in the period thanks to increasing orders. It estimated a net profit of between 587 million yuan (US$88 million) and 717 million yuan, reversing a year-earlier loss, even excluding non-recurring gains.
Hygon Information, whose processors serve both general computing and AI workloads, projected revenue growth of 50 per cent to 64 per cent in the first nine months. It cited rising demand for high-end chips as customers increasingly choose domestic alternatives over foreign suppliers.
Storage giant Shenzhen Longsys Electronics said its net profit during the period could reach 14 billion to 14.9 billion yuan, roughly 20 times the figure for the previous year. It noted that price increases for DRAM and NAND flash storage had slowed in the third quarter, giving profits a smaller boost.
Memory prices could remain firm through 2027, according to a Morgan Stanley report on Sunday, which also warned that supply catching up or customers slowing their purchases could cool the boom even without weaker AI demand.
Optical module supplier Accelink Technologies forecast a nine-month net profit growth of 65 per cent to 82 per cent, citing both global AI capital spending and Chinese cloud providers’ continued investment in data centres as profit drivers.
Silicon wafer supplier Xian Eswin Material Technology said its production lines ran at full capacity in the first nine months, with sales volumes up about 43 per cent to 8.3 million wafers. Although its net profit of about 151 million yuan during the period was boosted by gains from investments in initial public offerings by its customers, it still expected a loss after excluding non-recurring items.
China’s AI buildout and efforts to replace imported processors are bringing more business to local chip designers. Research firm TrendForce projected in August that Chinese-designed chips would account for almost 90 per cent of the country’s high-end AI processor market this year.
The growth in chip production is also lifting materials suppliers. Hubei Feilihua Quartz Glass forecast nine-month net profit growth of 35 per cent to 56 per cent, citing stronger semiconductor demand and opportunities to replace imported products.
The research firm Bernstein said in a Tuesday report that quartz components used in chipmaking equipment were already well localised in China, with further growth increasingly tied to orders for domestic chipmaking equipment.
Howard Liu is a Beijing-based technology and business reporter at the South China Morning Post, covering the semiconductor industry, AI and global tech supply chains. Previously at Caixin Media, he focused on China’s AI, semiconductor and cloud computing sectors. A graduate of Columbia University, he enjoys running, swimming and hiking.

"As of now it is too early to make that call, but we are formulating that proposal now which will be submitted. The fund allocation will be comparable with the earlier phase," Waghmare added.
In December 2018, the Cabinet approved the National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber-Physical Systems (NM-ICPS) for an initial five-year term with an outlay of ₹3,660 crore. Union Minister Jitendra Singh-led Department of Science & Technology is implementing this Mission.
"The National Quantum Mission (NQM) is the youngest. We are in the third year now, and it has done a brilliant job in certain directions. In quantum communication, we have made good leaps. DST supports exploratory research," Waghmare said.
In April 2023, the Cabinet approved NQM for the 2023–24 to 2030–31 period with a budget allocation of ₹6,003.65 crore.
The NQM is one of nine initiatives under Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Science, Technology Innovation Advisory Council (PMSTIAC), aimed at positioning India as a global leader in quantum technology.
Under the national program, dedicated efforts are underway to develop quantum-resilient encryption techniques and post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) frameworks, ensuring the safety and sovereignty of the country's critical database systems in the quantum era.
"One of our mandates and emphasis is the translation of research into real-world products and applications, and that was historically a weak part in the Indian community, but the department was actually very visionary."

India aims to take R&D investment to 2% of the GDP by 2035.
The Technology, Translation and Innovation (TTI) division under the department has been actively engaged across the entire value chain, and supports moderate funding. "If you want to now scale up and make real-world applications and products which will be sold globally, then you need industries to come in and invest."

Waghmare further said that quantum communication is one of the major outcomes, following the demonstration of a 1,000-kilometer network, and efforts are underway to also demonstrate a 2,000-kilometer quantum communication network.
The milestone was achieved using an indigenous Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) network developed by QNu Labs, a Bengaluru-based deep-tech startup.

indian-startups-ac92425b30.headline: Even Benchmark thinks AI is eroding the venture pact against backing rivals
indian-startups-ac92425b30.fulltext:
For decades, the unwritten rule of venture capital was that a firm doesn’t back two companies that compete head-on. But speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this week, the partners of Benchmark readily acknowledged that the AI boom is straining that rule.
It’s been on the verge of snapping for some time. The towering AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic share dozens of the same investors at this point. Then, at the end of September, Factory, a startup that builds an AI agent to write software, said it was firing board observer and adviser Chris Degnan for “unethical conduct involving Cognition,” its direct rival and the maker of the Devin coding agent. Factory’s CEO alleged Degnan had discussed a job at Cognition while privy to Factory’s board-level discussions. Degnan said he had already resigned and denied sharing anything confidential. Soon after, he announced he was joining Cognition as chief revenue officer. Powerhouse investor Vinod Khosla sided with Degnan on X, blasting Factory’s CEO and calling the company “a struggling second tier competitor.” Khosla Ventures backs both companies.
Even Benchmark, a firm whose reputation rests on 10- to 15-year partnerships with founders at the earliest stage, said the old rule can no longer be counted on. Asked at Disrupt whether the pact against backing rivals still holds as portfolio companies expand into each other’s territory, its partners described the conflicts as a matter of necessity, not preference.
“The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly,” said Eric Vishria. Companies pivot and change, he said, and “you are going to get conflicts, and that’s just the reality of the current dynamic.”
Vishria said Benchmark stays committed to each founder and keeps what it learns confidential, and he downplayed how much a VC could pass along anyway: “We are not product or technology experts.” Seemingly referring to the Factory-Cognition dispute, he said Benchmark has been fortunate not to land in “that type of insane direct conflict.” Exclusivity, he said, remains “really important” at the very early stage Benchmark favors. “But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.”
Chetan Puttagunta said AI is accelerating the problem. As the cost of building software “effectively goes to zero,” he said, founders are “incredibly ambitious.” Because they now see a “surface area” and want to claim all of it, he continued, “[i]t’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other.”
He drew a line between a direct competitor at the outset, which he called “an easy answer,” and a portfolio company that expands into another’s turf over time. “That happens,” he said.
Peter Fenton called the issue “kryptonite” and the firm’s toughest problem. He described a spectrum of how investors relate to their companies. At one end is the co-founder, who would never work on a competing company. At the other is the public-market stock picker, who can own several rivals because he is merely allocating capital, not shaping any of them. Benchmark sits nearer the co-founder end, Fenton said, and treats transparency as a golden rule. “There shouldn’t be the surprise after the fact.” If a conflict does emerge, a founder should never feel shortchanged, he added.
Benchmark isn’t declaring the pact dead. At the same time, when a firm that built its name on loyalty says conflicts are coming, founders might rightly wonder who else will be this candid.

global-economics-60328f5d25.headline: Services exports decline marginally in September amid AI-led muted growth of IT and software services

global-economics-60328f5d25.fulltext:
India’s services exports in September fell marginally by about 0.87 per cent year-on-year to $36.4 billion signalling slowdown in IT and IT-enabled services, which make up a chunk of the country’s services exports. Analysts predict that slowing demand for IT services in the Western world, advancements in AI and the impact of geopolitical shifts on travel and logistics services, could be among key reasons.
India’s services exports, however, grew 8.7 per cent YoY to $216.3 billion in April–September 2026, Ministry of Commerce data released on Thursday show. However, the Ministry notes that data for services sector for September are an estimation as RBI, which tracks services exports data, has only put out data till August.
businessline analysis of RBI data on services exports (the latest of which is August) shows that services exports saw a YoY monthly decline before this only in March 2024.
“With the US, EU and UK making up almost 85 per cent of the services exports, any shift or slowdown from these regions drives momentum loss in exports,” Ajay Srivastava, founder, Global Trade Research Initiative, said. “The ongoing inflation and elevated interest rates in the US and Europe have led global Fortune 500 clients to slash discretionary IT budgets, defer non-essential digital transformations, and emphasise cost-optimisation contracts,” he added.
Simultaneously, advancements in AI tools and automation are also shrinking billing hours and contract sizes across routine software maintenance, and traditional IT-enabled/BPO services, Srivastava said.
Ajay Sahai, Director General & CEO, Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO), told businessline that the decline could be a combination of a high base, IT services slowdown, and impact of geopolitical conflicts on travel and tourism services.
American companies, who are major consumers of India’s services, are going through slowdown and all the war-related tensions have made travel and logistics more difficult, he said. “However, given the job scenario, it is good news that merchandise exports, especially the more labour-intensive industries, are doing well,” he added.
Another tech analyst said that business services, which mainly comprises global capability centre (GCCs), have also been going slow in expansion in the last few months, and have been prioritising internal productivity led by AI. Similarly, revenue growth of IT majors has also been mute as they grapple with AI-led deflation in contracts and top line with many of them leaning on acquisitions to show inorganic growth, the person added.
Export of services has been on a growth path for India with some analysts also pointing out that they were close to equalling merchandise exports in a few years. Services exports had also touched an all-time high of $421.3 billion in FY26 and were up nearly 9 per cent YoY from $387.5 billion in FY25).
Given this trend, the marginal decline of services exports, comprising IT and IT-enabled services, software, business services, and other exports, is in focus and will be closely watched in coming months.

agritech-c1685182d9.headline: India's Monsoon rainfall 15% below normal between onset & withdrawal
agritech-c1685182d9.fulltext:
India received 76.86 cm rainfall between June 4 and October 15 when the south-west monsoon was active over the country, which is 15 per cent below its long period average of 90.63 cm, according to India Meteorological Department (IMD) data. The south-west monsoon, after its onset over Keralam on June 4, withdrew from the entire country on October 15.
During this period, except the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which reported 1 per cent surplus rainfall, all the meteorological sub-divisions in the south peninsula region were deficient, with a shortfall between 23 per cent and 46 per cent. As the North-East monsoon has now set in, these sub-divisions look forward to getting some rains to help the crops in winter season, particularly in non-irrigated areas.
In Central India where monsoon rainfall was 6 per cent below normal, except Maharashtra and Goa, which were deficient, all other states had either normal or excess rainfall. Maharashtra has reported 23 per cent deficit and Goa 36 per cent. On the other hand, Odisha received 23 per cent surplus rains, whereas Chhattisgarh 2 per cent shortfall. Madhya Pradesh had 7 per cent deficit and Gujarat 12 per cent below normal.
Most deficient
The north-west India too received 6 per cent below normal rains like Central India. Among the major agricultural states in this region, Punjab (-37 per cent), Haryana (-21 per cent) and Rajasthan (-24 per cent) reported deficient rainfall while Uttar Pradesh (+6 per cent) had normal precipitation.
The east and north-east region was 27 per cent deficient as Arunachal Pradesh (-45 per cent), Assam (-29 per cent), Bihar (-32 per cent) and Meghalaya (-61 per cent) had less rainfall. But, West Bengal has reported 2 per cent deficit and Jharkhand 6 per cent deficit rainfall between June 4 and October 15.
Across the country, Ladakh has received maximum 112 per cent above normal rainfall while Meghalaya the lowest 61 per cent below normal rainfall. In quantitative value among the states, Goa has received 196.68 cm rainfall, which is the highest in the country, while Punjab reported 28 cm, the lowest.

Rajasthan's kharif crop output is expected to decline due to deficient monsoon rains, with bajra and guar production projected to fall, while groundnut output may rise.

Production of kharif crops in Rajasthan is expected to decline due to deficient monsoon rains, a senior official of the Agriculture department said.
“The production estimates for the kharif 2026 season indicate a decline in the production of key crops such as bajra (pearl millet), moong (green gram) and guar (cluster bean). Conversely, groundnut production among oilseeds may fare slightly better than in the previous year,” the official said.
He pointed out that the final figures were yet to be confirmed, as crop arrivals at the mandis (commodity markets) were still under way.
According to the department’s estimates, bajra was sown across 3.958 million hectares in the state this year, with production projected at 4.939 million tonnes. In contrast, the previous year saw sowing across 4.352 million hectares, with production of 5.373 million tonnes.

On October 8, the US Department of Labour decided to stop processing PERM labour-certification requests from eight technology firms, including Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. The Department of Labor said it would neither accept new applications nor process pending applications involving the named companies.
PERM, or Program Electronic Review Management, is the initial step in the employment-based green-card process for most immigrants applying under the EB-2 and EB-3 categories. In order to proceed to the next stage, employers are required to prove that they have tried to hire Americans for the jobs in question.
The processing of the applications has been suspended in accordance with 20 CFR § 656.31(b), which allows for the temporary interruption of services if there are grounds to believe that fraud or wilful misrepresentation is involved.
Notwithstanding the administration’s justification, it is important to study how allegations must not be confused with provided proof of fraudulent activity. Vice President JD Vance accused companies that employ people on H-1B visas of creating a caste of foreign indentured servants.
On the heels of the H-1B controversy came reports of investigations into the J-1 visa program, which have seen the involvement of dozens of American universities. In the context of Vance’s comments on H-1B visas and intensified scrutiny of J-1, the latest development suggest that the debate over America’s immigration policy and the prospects of its labour market will continue to gain momentum. This would, in the meantime, systematically erode India’s IT service sector’s integrative loop with American companies and vice-versa.
The stages of the H-1B-to-green-card process could therefore be described as entering the United States, living there as a worker, and eventually receiving permanent residency. Each of these possesses its own restrictions.
Successful applicants
Indian nationals comprise a significant part of successful H-1B applicants. A US Citizenship and Immigration Services’ FY2024 H-1B characteristics report says, Indians comprised 71% of successful applicants in 2024.
The immigration system has also become more expensive and unpredictable: the $100,000 H-1B fine announced in September 2025 was later clarified by USCIS to be applicable only to petitions made after September 21, 2025, as a one-time payment rather than an annual renewal.
This has become an IT programme. Infotech workers made up 32% of H-1B holders in fiscal 2003 and averaged over 65% across the last five fiscal years. H-1B status permits temporary employment, subject to immigration rules and the conditions of the petition. Workers may continue working lawfully while their green-card applications are delayed, provided their existing authorisation remains valid.
Program Electronic Review Management, or PERM, falls under the third category, which concerns the transition from being a temporary resident to receiving permanent residency. The suspension interrupts a stage of the process for affected applications, potentially delaying workers’ transition to permanent residency. Its consequences depend on the status of each application.
The size of the employment-based immigration backlog explains why the PERM suspension impacts individual workers: its immediate relevance for corporate profits is limited.
The Cato Institute estimated the US employment-based waiting list to contain approximately 1.8 million people in 2023, around 1.1 million of whom are Indians. This puts the portion of Indians in the queue at around 68%. The report estimated the time necessary to clear the backlog for Indian applicants to be up to 134 years with approximately 424,000 Indians dying before obtaining a visa.
This might have more of an impact than it seems, as permanent residency is a significant factor in the worker’s life, affecting their decision-making and planning. Another obstacle in their employment-based residency application might disrupt their lives severely.
Erosion of revenues
An RBI survey tracks an erosion in on-site revenues, from US$19 billion to US$18.4 billion. These are wages paid to staff members who work at client facilities overseas. The reduction implies that the traditional approach of sending numerous Indian professionals to work overseas is being de-emphasised relative to other approaches to technology services delivery. The larger industry trends confirm this shift.
Nasscom data reveals that Indian IT revenue totalled $315 billion in FY2025-26, up 6.1%, with exports of $246 billion, up 5.6%. The industry employed some 5.95 million workers and created about 135,000 net jobs in the past fiscal year. An American client can continue to buy software development, consulting, maintenance and other tech services from an Indian team without requiring those professionals to be based inside America.
A restriction on permanent residency might well impose genuine costs on workers while having limited impact on the revenue-generating capabilities of their employers. The differential impact will vary from company to company, project to project, and staffing model to staffing model, but the nuance explains how the market’s response to the policy change need not reflect the impact on individual workers’ circumstances.
For Indian IT companies, the PERM freeze may prove a small financial blow rather than a major threat to their business model. Most of their American revenue streams do not rely on having every employee on their payroll based in the US, and the fall in on-site earnings suggests an industry growing more capable of providing services beyond borders.
For Indian professionals, the implications are more personal. A green-card process that already takes years to complete has just become even more unpredictable for those considering applying, and for whose employers are affected. Even if their American jobs are unaffected, their plans for permanent residency may be set back.
And for India, the long-term impact is harder to assess. Restrictions on immigration may motivate multinational companies to invest more in local infrastructure, creating jobs and cementing India’s role as a centre for tech production. But it would also shift work away from Indian outsourcing firms and towards the captive centres of their American clients.
The short-term financial pain may be minimal.
The anxiety for those affected is however far greater. And the longer-term challenge will be whether the US can prevent a rush to move work to where it will have value, by closing access to where it currently does.
This moment also marks a troubling low-threshold point in US-India relations almost causing an irreparable harm to the long decadal diplomatic relationship between the two countries.
First, tariffs on Indian imports, and now restrictions on skilled human capital mobility from India to American companies could erode and dismantle core areas of economic integration between the two countries which was cementing a strong political bond as well. Where this leaves India and its economic integration strategy viz-a-viz the US (amidst a more conflicting relationship with China) should trouble policymakers than it seems to do in the current scenario.

ai-21e3505542.fulltext:
Meta has launched what it calls the “most capable” open-weight model in the United States. Dubbed Muse Spark Open, the model also has the distinction of having been designed to work with Macs.
The new model, which leverages 816 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window, claims to offer superior performance to other popular open-weight models, according to evaluation results released by Meta on Thursday.
Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and built for complex coding tasks and agentic labor. It has also been designed to run locally on Apple’s computers. However, you will still need a lot of power to run the model locally, with a requirement of at least 1 terabyte of RAM, per Engadget. The model will run best via the Mac Studio that comes equipped with the M5 Ultra chip.
Still, if you can muster the memory, Muse Spark Open may prove a significant work horse for coding and other desktop tasks. Meta says that it paired the model with Muse Code, its AI coding terminal, and deployed it to various agentic workflows, including coding fixes for a Mastodon client that included “bug fixes, new features, [and] full build.”
The company says it also deployed it in the service of running DaVinci Resolve, the high-end video editing software, revealing that the model was capable of reviewing and cropping footage.
Open-weight models provide a number of distinct industry advantages that aren’t afforded by closed and proprietary models. Open-weight models can be significantly more cost-efficient and can also offer transparency and flexibility that closed source models don’t allow.
Meta is making the new model available now through a number of different API platforms.

deep-tech-37913afbcf.headline: ISRO completes Gaganyaan module separation tests ahead of 2026 mission
deep-tech-37913afbcf.fulltext:
The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has successfully completed a series of Crew Module (CM)-Service Module (SM) separation tests for the Gaganyaan programme, validating the design adequacy of the separation system ahead of the first uncrewed mission, G1, which is targeted for launch in 2026.
Tests validate separation system design
The Gaganyaan Orbital Module comprises the Crew Module and the Service Module, which are connected through a separation system. Electrical and fluid servicing between the two modules is ensured through umbilical connections.
The modules are integrated before launch and function as a single unit from launch until the completion of the on-orbit phase of the mission. Before re-entry into Earth’s atmosphere, the Crew Module separates from the Service Module through a series of precisely sequenced events involving pyrotechnic devices and jettisoning systems.
To validate the overall design of the separation system, ISRO conducted the tests at the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC) in Thiruvananthapuram. The test setup simulated the integrated Crew Module-Service Module assembly and incorporated extensive instrumentation to assess the separation process.
The tests simulated the separation of the two modules, including the severing of multiple umbilical connections between them.
Critical Crew Module systems demonstrate robustness
According to ISRO, the tests not only validated the design adequacy of the separation system but also demonstrated the robustness and shock-survivability of several critical Crew Module subsystems.
These include avionics systems, inertial navigation systems, the Thermal Protection System in the aft and conical heat shields, the Crew Module Deployable Umbilical Shield, and pyrotechnic devices associated with the Crew Module Uprighting System and the Thermal and Humidity Control System.
Successful tests boost confidence ahead of G1 mission
The successful completion of the tests provides confidence in the functioning of the implemented separation system for the upcoming first uncrewed Gaganyaan mission, G1, which is targeted for launch in 2026.
Published on October 17, 2026

Pune-Based Muks Robotics Secures ISRO Project to Develop SPACEO Prime, an Indian Humanoid Space Worker
PNN
Pune (Maharashtra) [India], October 16: Muks Robotics, a Pune-based humanoid robotics company, has secured a project with the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) to develop SPACEO Prime, India’s first humanoid space worker. The project marks a milestone in the Indian Space Economy to develop intelligent robots capable of operating in space.
As space missions become increasingly complex, robotic systems could play an important role in assisting astronauts, performing demanding operations and handling tasks in hazardous environments. For Muks Robotics, the project represents progress towards a vision first conceived by its founder, Dr. Mukesh Bangar, in 2021: building humanoids not just for Earth, but also for space.
Muks Robotics is a Pune-based startup, working towards the development of humanoid robots and Physical AI systems designed to perceive their surroundings, understand instructions, and perform tasks in real-world environments.
Developing a humanoid for space-related applications presents challenges beyond conventional robotics. Mobility, manipulation, autonomy, and reliability must be considered alongside the demands of the intended operating environment. The ISRO project provides an opportunity for Muks Robotics to build indigenous humanoids in alignment with “Atmanirbhar Bharat,” strengthening India’s self-reliance in advanced robotics and contributing to the nation’s vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.
At the centre of the company’s journey is Dr. Mukesh Bangar, Founder and CEO of Muks Robotics. A self-taught AI and robotics engineer, Dr. Bangar is focused on developing intelligent robotic systems capable of understanding their surroundings, learning autonomously, and performing meaningful physical tasks.
“I firmly believe that true freedom from pain and suffering (Moksh) can be achieved through self-sustaining autonomous robots. Moreover, now is the right time to deploy conscious, intelligent robots to other planets to safeguard the future of our existence,” says Dr. Mukesh Bangar.
In 2021, his vision began taking shape around a long-term ambition to build humanoids for Earth and beyond. The company subsequently presented its mission and vision through a video in 2023, outlining its direction in humanoid robotics and its ambition to extend robotic capabilities beyond Earth.
The development of the SPACEO platform created a foundation for pursuing this ambition. The ISRO project represents a significant step towards translating that vision into a dedicated humanoid development effort, bringing the company closer to its goal of developing robots capable of supporting human activities in space.
The development of SPACEO Prime aligns with India’s Make in India initiative and Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s vision of Viksit Bharat 2047, which aims to transform India into a developed nation by the centenary of its independence. The vision emphasises self-reliance, innovation and indigenous technological advancement.
With established capabilities in satellite technology, launch systems and planetary exploration, India is well-positioned to expand into advanced robotics, artificial intelligence and autonomous systems. For Muks Robotics, SPACEO Prime represents an effort to develop advanced humanoid technology in India and contribute to the country’s growing deep-tech ecosystem. However, developing a space-oriented humanoid requires rigorous testing, reliability and safety to meet the demanding conditions of space missions.
Humanoid robots could offer advantages in environments designed around human tools, workstations, and equipment. Their articulated arms and human-like body structure could potentially enable them to manipulate objects, handle tools, and interact with existing infrastructure.
Future applications could include equipment inspection, maintenance assistance, material handling, and other repetitive or hazardous tasks. Such systems could help reduce astronauts’ exposure to certain risks and support mission operations.
These possibilities depend on the robot’s capabilities, engineering validation, and mission requirements. They represent the broader potential of humanoid space robotics rather than confirmed operational capabilities of SPACEO Prime.
Muks Robotics aims to build humanoids for practical applications on Earth while developing the technological foundations for future work beyond the planet.
SPACEO Prime brings together this long-term vision and an opportunity to contribute to India’s space technology ambitions. Moving from development to actual space operations will require sustained engineering, testing, and validation.
For a robotics company based in Pune, the ambition now extends beyond conventional workplaces. With a vision of extending its mission to the Moon and Mars as well. What began as a vision in 2021 is taking shape as a dedicated development effort, with the potential to expand the role of Indian-built humanoid technology beyond Earth.
For Muks Robotics, the goal is not simply to build a machine that resembles a human, but to develop one that could help humans work in places where they have never worked before.

global-economics-b7ab1b26ee.headline: AI startup RapidCanvas raises $29 million led by Vertex Ventures
global-economics-b7ab1b26ee.fulltext:
RapidCanvas, a managed artificial intelligence execution company, has raised $29 million in a Series B funding round led by Vertex Ventures SEA & India, the startup announced on Friday.
Hitachi Ventures joined the company's cap table, while existing investors Accel, Peak XV Partners, Valley Capital Partners and Titanium Ventures also participated in the round. With the latest investment, RapidCanvas has raised a total of $52.5 million.
The company will use the funding to expand its go-to-market teams and network of private equity and advisory partners. It also plans to grow its field AI engineering team across India, the US and Brazil.
"AI can be the great equalizer, but so far its biggest wins have gone to the Fortune 100. We want to give every enterprise the same opportunity," said Rahul Pangam, co-founder and chief executive of RapidCanvas, in a statement. “Vibe coding has made it easy to start building with AI. Getting AI into production reliably and safely still remains the biggest gap.”
Global spending on direct AI services will reach $516 billion by 2029, with a compound annual growth rate of 14.7% over five years, according to a Gartner note published in January. RapidCanvas' competitors Databricks, Altair, and Quantexa, among others.
AI execution gap
The funding comes as venture capital firms increasingly back companies seeking to disrupt traditional services markets, which have long been dominated by a handful of large players.
RapidCanvas is targeting businesses with annual revenues ranging from $100 million to $10 billion. Many of these companies have already carved out mandates for AI implementation, creating an opportunity for firms that can help turn experimentation into practical business applications.
In India, large enterprises that have traditionally been slow to adopt new technologies from startup vendors have begun moving faster, as interest in deploying AI grows.
“Most enterprises are still searching for real returns on their AI spend. RapidCanvas delivers them by pairing an AI platform that compounds with every deployment and forward-deployed engineers who own the outcome end to end,” said Piyush Kharbanda, general partner at Vertex Ventures SEA & India, in a statement.
RapidCanvas' estimated revenue as of December 2025 stood at $35.8 million, according to Tracxn.
AI-led disruption of the services sector has become a broader area of interest for India's venture investors. Funds such as Bessemer Venture Partners, Lightspeed, Stellaris Venture Partners, Accel and TVS Capital Funds have been actively investing in companies looking to challenge traditional services models. Last year, Bessemer unveiled a roadmap outlining how it expects AI to disrupt the IT services sector.
RapidCanvas pairs its AI platform with field AI engineers to deliver custom AI solutions. AI engineers learn each customer's business processes, design and build custom AI applications, and stay accountable for the applications' outcomes after delivery.

world-eb49429591.fulltext:
[Text below is CNN's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Police detained India’s “cockroach” movement founder Abhijeet Dipke and some supporters on Friday, ahead of a protest called by him in capital Delhi’s central business district, the latest rally to demand the resignation of India’s election chief.
The youth-led “Cockroach Janta Party” (CJP), opposition groups, and student organizations have held almost daily protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
More than 130 million voters were deleted during the revision but the Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol. The BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Dipke called Friday’s protest in support of two CJP leaders detained and sent to jail this week for five days for demonstrating at a protest site in violation of a ban.
The group and left-wing student organisations had urged supporters to gather at the Central Park in New Delhi’s busy Connaught Place shopping and food district on Friday evening to wave and hoist the national flag.
Police say they warned movement leader against protesting
The live video on CJP’s Instagram handle showed Dipke coming out of a house and walking towards the street, where police officers stopped him and, after a brief argument, hauled him into a police car and drove away.
“We are detaining you right now,” a police officer could be heard telling Dipke.
“I have not broken any law right now…how can you detain me,” Dipke asked the police officers as he was taken away.
There was no immediate comment from the police on the detention.
“Abhijeet is detained by Delhi Police,” CJP posted on X. “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”
Student activist Neha Bora, a prominent face of the protests, was also detained as she tried to reach Connaught Place with dozens of supporters, local media reported.
Earlier on Friday, police met Dipke and warned him against going ahead with the protest. Security was stepped up and the park itself shut by civic authorities.
Senior police officer Sachin Sharma told news agency ANI that Dipke was served a notice that asked him to obey the law, and that he was informed of the implications of any violations.
Television images showed dozens of people arriving at Connaught Place amid heavy security, some of them waving small versions of the national flag.
Small protests were also held in financial capital Mumbai and tech hub Bengaluru, while student organizations held a demonstration in the eastern city of Patna, with people waving flags of their organizations and pushing against police barricades.
Youth used as pawns, BJP says
The cockroach movement has emerged as one of the biggest political challenges faced by Modi and his BJP in his 12 years in power.
A weeks-long sit-in by its supporters earlier this year forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation over exam paper leaks.
The latest demonstrations erupted after the Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar’s two deputies raised concerns internally about voter list changes, registration procedures and digital systems.
The 130 million names that were removed from voter lists starting last year — equivalent to more than the population of Japan — included 28 million people who had died, 63 million who relocated, and 30 million who could not be traced, according to the Election Commission.
Opposition parties allege the deletions disproportionately affect Muslims and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, allegations the commission and the BJP reject.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said the demonstrations were the main opposition Congress party’s attempt to “seize power”.
“Instead of channeling the energy of the youth toward nation-building, they are being used as pawns in the politics of anarchy,” he said at a media briefing on Friday.
This story has been updated with additional developments.

global-economics-47ff5dc261.headline: From Operation Sindoor to ADAS: Tonbo Imaging takes battlefield technology to civilian applications
global-economics-47ff5dc261.source: Business News Today: Latest Business News, Finance News
global-economics-47ff5dc261.fulltext:
From countering Pakistan’s drone offensive during India’s Operation Sindoor to detecting pedestrians and cattle on dark highways and elephants along Assam’s railway corridors, military-grade imaging technology is finding potential civilian applications. Bengaluru-based Tonbo Imaging is looking to adapt its battlefield surveillance and targeting expertise for advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and railway safety, opening new opportunities ahead of its ₹852-crore IPO on October 15.
Tonbo’s MGS-23 equips conventional anti-aircraft guns with thermal imaging and targeting capabilities, while it develops WaveStrike high-power microwave technology to turn off drone swarms by disrupting their electronics.
Asked about Operation Sindoor, a source familiar with Tonbo’s defence programmes declined to share operational details, citing strict military non-disclosure agreements, but said its technologies had been deployed across multiple military theatres and demonstrated operational readiness under battlefield conditions.
“We don’t make the weapon; we make the eyes and the brains of the weapon,” the source said.
FROM FIGHTER JETS TO MISSILE SEEKERS
India’s modernisation of the Su-30MKI fighter aircraft offers a potential market for Tonbo’s electro-optical and infrared technologies. Such systems help aircraft detect, identify and track targets in poor visibility, integrating with targeting pods and missile guidance systems to improve precision strikes.
Tonbo has supplied seeker-related technology for missile programmes involving Bharat Dynamics, although it has not disclosed a direct Su-30MKI integration contract.
Tonbo Imaging develops electro-optical sights, driver-vision systems, and thermal imaging payloads for precision targeting on military platforms built by partners including Larsen & Toubro (L&T) and DRDO. The Arjun Mk1A tank features a remote-controlled weapon station for its 12.7-mm machine gun, while Tonbo separately markets compact thermal weapon sights for rifles and sniper systems under its proprietary ‘Arjun’ brand.
Sources expect missile seekers to become a significant revenue driver around FY29, followed by high-power microwave systems during FY29–30. WaveStrike remains at the prototype stage.
BATTLEFIELD EYES FOR CIVILIAN ROADS
The same ability to identify heat signatures and track moving targets could help vehicles detect hazards beyond headlights.
“An elephant is one big thermal signature,” the source said, explaining that thermal imaging could alert locomotive drivers to animals crossing railway tracks, particularly along Assam’s wildlife corridors, where Tonbo is in an advanced pilot project with Indian Railways, according to sources familiar with the development.
Tonbo is exploring railway safety systems that combine thermal imaging, electro-optical sensors, and radar, alongside ADAS applications for passenger cars, commercial trucks, and mining equipment.
“The shortest-term opportunity in automotive or transportation in India is in the heavy-vehicle sector,” the source said.
“We understood two domains very well. We understood defence and we understood autonomous vehicles,” the source added.
ORDER BOOK, REVENUE AND IPO
Tonbo has a signed order book of approximately ₹290 crore, excluding defence programmes undergoing qualification and commercial negotiations, according to people familiar with its operations.
People familiar with its growth plans said revenue could cross ₹550 crore in FY27 and approach ₹1,000 crore in FY28, up from FY26 turnover of ₹362.65 crore. These estimates are not formal company guidance.
The ₹852-crore IPO is entirely an offer for sale, allowing early investors, including Celesta Capital and Edelweiss, to exit without raising fresh capital for Tonbo.
Investors including SBI Mutual Fund, Amansa, ValueQuest, 360 ONE, HDFC Life and Malabar participated in pre-IPO transactions worth approximately ₹400 crore, according to people familiar with the deals.
“Let us deliver on this business,” the source said, suggesting fresh fundraising could follow as revenue scales.
